title: Teen who singer D4vd is accused of killing had multiple abortions, texts reveal
description: WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of
body: WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of murdering, reveal she had been pregnant and had had an abortion before her death. The messages were shown during a hearing for a judge to determine if the singer, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, should go on trial for the teen's death last year."What [if] the first abortion didn't work?" Celeste texted Burke in June 2024, according to prosecutors. She was 13 years old at the time and he was 19. Prosecutors say Burke killed her after she threatened to reveal he had been abusing a minor and destroy his career. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing the girl.In an exchange from January 2024, Burke apologised to the teen for "putting her through this", according to messages shown in the Los Angeles court on Friday.She responded, "neither of us are capable of watching and taking care of the baby. it's for the best no?"Burke asked, "also my mother always told me to ask this question if I was ever in this situation … it is mine right?" Celeste replied "of course its yours David", according to testimony from a detective.The court heard that in another text to the teen, sent in June 2024, Burke wrote: "Let's let this abortion be the last one til we have the real one…" Prosecutors presented iCloud data recovered from the defendant's iPhone, showing texts between him and Celeste dating back to 8 August 2022, when she was 11 years old and he was 17.The device belonging to Burke also had photos of the teenager during the alleged sexual abuse, prosecutors and Los Angeles Police Detective Corey Farell said on Friday.The victim's mother, Mercedes Rivas Hernandez, became visibly emotional and left the court with her husband as details of some of the pictures were described during the proceedings. Burke's phone also showed conversations the two had had about moving in together, which they had dubbed "Operation Awesome".The pair "broke up" in November 2024, but stayed in contact, according to a memo filed by prosecutors earlier this year. Prosecutors allege they argued on the night before her death, allegedly over Burke's relationships with other women.Dr Grant Ho of the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner, who conducted the post-mortem examination on Celeste, also testified on Friday.Ho told the court it was "extremely difficult to tell" exactly when the girl died, owing to the state of decomposition when her remains were found.Lawyers for the defence seized on that uncertainty, questioning whether it was possible that the teenager could have somehow harmed herself. Farrell, the police detective, testified that DNA taken from blood found in Burke's Hollywood Hills home and garage was a match for Celeste.D4vd, who rose to fame on TikTok with the viral hits Romantic Homicide and Here With Me, was on tour when police found Celeste's body in the front boot of his Tesla in September 2025 - the day after she would have turned 15. His worldwide tour was cancelled and he largely retreated from public life and social media.Police announced his arrest in April this year.Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman has filed seven criminal charges against him, including murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child and the mutilation of remains.They said the teen was reported missing by her family and was last seen at Burke's home on 3 April 2025 - five months before her remains were discovered in the Tesla.Prosecutors have said he met Celeste online when she was 11, and allege he started sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18. Friday marked the fourth day of testimony in the pre-trial hearing. Earlier revelations by prosecutors included that Hernandez had been brought by Burke to London and Texas to meet members of his family there. Testimony is expected to resume on Monday.

schema.headline: Teen who singer D4vd is accused of killing had multiple abortions, texts reveal

title: Trump orders Smithsonian to post warnings about 'inaccurate' US history
description: President Donald Trump has ordered signs to be placed outside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, to caution visitors about exhibits
body: President Donald Trump has ordered signs to be placed outside the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, to caution visitors about exhibits his administration views as "inaccurate".The order directs the Department of Interior to issue the warnings, and also to direct people about where they can find "accurate information regarding America's history".The Trump administration has often accused the Smithsonian Institution, the world's largest research museum, as well as other academic organisations of harbouring an anti-American bias.The Smithsonian did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment. The order on Friday - titled Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution - accuses museum leadership of not doing enough to celebrate America's founders on the country's 250th anniversary of independence, which took place on 4 July.It says the museum's leadership team "views American history as a 'prime tool' to advance ideas of social justice and the radical transformation of our society".An accompanying White House statement, external also accused the museum of  veering "toward extreme political activism, rooted in Marxism, to divide, dispirit, and discourage Americans".Democrats who oversee the Smithsonian condemned the order."This EO is a clear political overreach, driven by an ideological agenda to rewrite American history," congresswoman Melanie Stansbury, ranking member of the House Administration Committee, wrote on X. "Our Smithsonian institutions do not belong to the President, but to the American people and so does our nation's history."The executive order comes just days after Smithsonian director Anthea Hartig was grilled by Republican lawmakers in two congressional hearings, where the museum was accused of being "infected by a woke ideology that seeped into public displays, educational materials and planning documents".Earlier this month, the White House Domestic Policy Council released a scathing report, claiming that the museum "erases our heritage".Trump has set out to radically reshape American culture, which he says has been contaminated by "woke" left-wing ideology. He has signed several orders that are intended to eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion programmes from the federal government - some of which led to legal challenges.In March, he issued a separate order against the Smithsonian, directing it to "eliminate improper, divisive, or anti-American ideology".The Smithsonian is largely funded by the federal government. Its museums offer free entry to some 15 to 30 million visitors each year. It operates 21 museums in Washington, Virginia and New York.They include the National Museum of American History, the National Portrait Gallery, the American Art Museum, the National Zoo and more than a dozen others.

schema.headline: Trump orders Smithsonian to post warnings about 'inaccurate' US history

title: Heatwave reveals lost archaeological sites across Wales
description: RCAHMW said the east and north-east of Wales has been very dry since mid-May, while much of  west and south Wales stayed fairly damp and green.However
body: RCAHMW said the east and north-east of Wales has been very dry since mid-May, while much of  west and south Wales stayed fairly damp and green.However, the series of heatwaves in late June scorched off grasslands across Wales.It revealed "monuments ranging from prehistoric long barrows and forts to Roman buildings and even First World War practice trenches," they said.  The national archive for the Welsh historic environment has released photographs of Driver's discoveries following flights from Haverfordwest and Caernarfon airport in June and July. "This year has been pretty windy across Wales, so some of the longer trips to record cropmarks have made for challenging flying," Driver said.   "Sometimes the cropmarks are so clear they jump out as we orbit the aircraft around to photograph them. But some parts of Wales are now so dry that the cropmarks can be faint and pretty hard to see."He added: "In these cases we digitally rebalance the colour bands of the image,  really making the archaeology 'pop' and reveal previously hidden details – these images appear as black and white".

schema.headline: Heatwave reveals lost archaeological sites across Wales

title: Ukraine's Zelensky struggles to fix crisis over removal of defence minister Fedorov
description: With an acting defence minister in place and a new commander-in-chief in charge of the military, Ukraine's recent political crisis is over, right?Not
body: With an acting defence minister in place and a new commander-in-chief in charge of the military, Ukraine's recent political crisis is over, right?Not so fast.The political fallout from President Volodymyr Zelensky's 15 July decision not to re-appoint Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister, as part of a cabinet reshuffle, continues to reverberate about Kyiv and beyond, even as air raid sirens wail and Russian drones and missiles are intercepted overhead.Fedorov's mostly young supporters are still mounting daily street protests, demanding that Zelensky reinstate the popular young innovator widely credited with driving much of Ukraine's recent technological innovation.On Thursday, Fedorov said he had rejected Zelensky's offers of alternative posts in government, saying there were only three positions worth having to influence the course of the war: minister of defence, commander-in-chief of the military or president of Ukraine."If you don't have a ministry under you, you don't have a budget," ex-deputy defence minister Alina Frolova said, "and you don't actually have the authority to do something."Fedorov's reference to the presidency did not go unnoticed. Was this the first public sign that the ousted minister sees himself as a rival to Zelensky?One former defence official suggested he became a real candidate for the presidency the moment he was dismissed.But with the country at war and no elections scheduled – Ukraine's constitution still prevents them in wartime – how useful is it to put your head above the political parapet so far in advance?"He's being childish," one opposition MP told me, on condition that he remained anonymous."He's looking to further his political career, which I think is just stupid in the circumstances where we are."The president's supporters say Zelensky has gone to great lengths to resolve the crisis, especially over the question of who to replace the unpopular commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi.Eventually he decided on Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43, a highly respected former commander of Ukraine's land forces."He consulted pretty much every significant figure in the Ukrainian army," former government adviser Yuriy Sak told the BBC earlier this week."So the decision that he has taken now is very well informed, and I support it because General Drapatyi is a young, battle-proven, modern general who will take our defences to a new level, hopefully."But while Drapatyi's appointment has been generally welcomed, it only represents a partial fix by a president scrambling to repair the damage caused by his removal of Fedorov.Ironically, for a president whose youth and apparent dynamism propelled him to power in 2019, Zelensky seems to have misjudged the mood of young Ukrainians, eager for their leaders – political and military – to represent their values and aspirations."It's quite natural that people want to see someone who is a warrior against corruption, who is very modern, who is young," Oleksandr Merezhko, an MP from Zelensky's Servant of the People party, said."People want to see something like that in politics, which they consider to be dirty and full of hypocrisy. They need heroes."But Merezhko agrees that Fedorov's ambitions and almost mythic, popular status may have brought about his downfall, especially for a president with a track record of sidelining those he sees as potential rivals."Don't outshine your master," Merezhko says, quoting from Robert Greene's 1998 self-help book, The 48 Laws of Power.Most analysts agree that last week's reshuffle had one overarching purpose: to cut Fedorov down to size. But Zelensky's strategy appears to have backfired."His removal has led to the opposite result," Merezhko says. "His rating soared. Just soared."Few doubt Fedorov's commitment, imagination and drive, but some question whether his outsized reputation is fully justified.They point out that he inherited a situation in which Ukraine had already successfully built up its medium- and long-range strike capabilities, something over which the defence minister has little day-to-day influence."The energy and clarity he brought to the job was impressive and he showed immense personal courage," a former European defence official said. "But the thing that will carry on regardless is the innovation culture. It's 2,000 companies, not a single individual."One opposition MP, who asked not to be identified, put it more bluntly."Ninety-nine per cent of these young people on the street have no clue how the ministry of defence is operating, how the general staff is operating," he said."They think Fedorov is good because he wants to fight with drones and Syrskyi was bad because he was looking for people to fight. It's a dramatic simplification which is totally wrong."But understandable, perhaps, in a country exhausted by 12 years of war with Russia. Who would not want to believe that drones and robots can do the job, rather than a member of your own family, roughly conscripted on the streets of your own hometown?Everyone agrees that Ukraine needs to put this politically toxic episode behind it before summer gives way to autumn and the country braces itself for another Russian assault on its energy grid."We need to prepare for how we will get through the winter," Zelensky said on the Telegram messaging app on Thursday.Politicians and experts interviewed for this piece mostly agree that while the political damage of this episode continues to undermine President Zelensky's authority and reputation, Ukraine is unlikely to experience significant setbacks on the battlefield.What Zelensky calls his "long-range sanctions" campaign against Russia is in full swing, causing mounting damage to the Russian economy. Ukraine's long front lines, meanwhile, remain largely static, thanks to a 15-30km (9-18-mile) wide "kill zone" where anything or anyone who moves is observed and attacked by drones.As a young, still relatively immature democracy, Ukraine's institutions have been put under colossal strain by Russia's full-scale invasion. But, many argue, the country remains resilient and resourceful."The secret of Ukraine's success is that we are much stronger horizontally than vertically," opposition MP Andrii Osadchuk told me."I hope the damage will be minimal."

schema.headline: Ukraine's Zelensky struggles to fix crisis over removal of defence minister Fedorov

title: Graduation outfits: Students tell us how to impress on a budget
description: "My mum is a designer so she made this for me," says Wendy. "It took her a week… I'm her daughter, so she had to put in every [effort]."Wendy says the
body: "My mum is a designer so she made this for me," says Wendy. "It took her a week… I'm her daughter, so she had to put in every [effort]."Wendy says the significance of graduation inspired her to create a custom look. "I feel like you have to because it's your day. We go through a lot to get a master's degree so you have to look your best on the day."Graduation also comes at a time when students are "the least financially resilient", says Allingham, as they have been absorbing the costs of studying all year.The maintenance loan falls short of living costs by an average of £502 per month, according to analysis by Save The Student, external. This gap is plugged - sometimes only partially - by parental support, part-time jobs and debt.Another factor that can increase the cost of graduation is buying an official photograph, with providers specified by your university, adds Allingham. "The price of photography on the day - it's extortionate."Professional packages at the University of Salford start at £30 - an image of the graduate is sent digitally - and the most expensive is £350. For that you receive about 20 prints with various mounts and frames of two images, one of the graduate and another with friends and family.Like Keerthana, Alicia Munhupedzi used the internet to find her dress - though it was a bit last minute."I thought, 'Where can I get a nice dress really quickly and cheaply?'" The answer? Depop, the second-hand clothing app popular among Gen Z shoppers that sold for $1.2bn (£890m) earlier this year.Like others, Alicia felt her outfit was important. "Graduation, it's a milestone thing, especially if you're not planning on doing a master's," she says. "So, to me, there was a pressure."So much so she couldn't sleep properly the night before her ceremony and woke at dawn to get ready. "I made it through today off two hours of sleep, water, good vibes, energy and a coffee."Knowing all eyes would be fixed on her when she was handed her degree, Keerthana says she was nervous for her graduation ceremony - but it passed more quickly than she thought it might."This is the only moment you get for yourself," she says. And was the 05:00 wake-up and two hours of getting ready worth it? "Yeah," Keerthana says, "I couldn't compromise on that."Additional reporting by Kate Berry and George Sandeman.

schema.headline: Graduation outfits: Students tell us how to impress on a budget

title: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids
description: Image source, Nilly DahliaImage caption, Nilly Dahlia says she wants her kids to enjoy a "nostalgic summer"ByEmily HoltThe six-week summer holidays ha
body: Image source, Nilly DahliaImage caption, Nilly Dahlia says she wants her kids to enjoy a "nostalgic summer"ByEmily HoltThe six-week summer holidays have officially begun and, for many parents, finding exciting but affordable activities for children can be tough. For most families in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the break has only just started. In Scotland, children have enjoyed some time off already, but will return to school earlier than those elsewhere in the UK.Here are five tips to help children get the most out of the next few weeks of summer. 1. Not every holiday has to be abroad A family's first instinct when summer is approaching may be to look at booking a trip abroad, but rising costs and travel expenses mean a holiday isn't feasible for everyone. Mags Rivett, director at Family Holiday Charity, which supports families with UK trips, says there are many benefits to arranging time away with children that don't require expensive travel. She says the social aspect of a holiday can help children develop their communication skills. "Lots of kids have never really had the opportunity to meet people outside of their own community," Rivett says. "But if you go somewhere that's got social facilities, it's a really important opportunity."She says getting recommendations from friends and family is a good place to start. Rivett gives the example of Skegness, a coastal holiday destination in Lincolnshire, accessible by train or coach, which her charity has supported families to visit.A family-of-four's accommodation in a holiday park there this August starts at around £750 for a week, while an off-peak return train from Manchester would cost around £280 for four.By contrast, a last-minute trip to Majorca for a family-of-four at that time starts from around £2,000. Better deals can usually be found booking further in advance.2. Prioritise the moments, not the cost Samantha Thomas, creator of Budget Mum UK, says she focuses on the time she can give her children, rather than the money she could spend on a day out. Thomas suggests focusing on your budget first to understand what you can comfortably spend, and then build your activities around that, to help remove any "stress or guilt" during the holidays. "Children don't need a six-week programme of expensive activities," Thomas says. "Some of the memories that they'll treasure most will come from simple things, like baking together or a picnic in the park, or building a den in the living room."Ingredients to bake fairy cakes with buttercream icing usually cost between £10 and £15 - depending on what you already have in the cupboard.For a picnic - or picky bits - prices can vary. But it can easily be done on a budget of around £5. Image source, Samantha ThomasImage caption, Samantha Thomas says treasured family memories can be created on a budgetTasneem Abdur-Rashid, an author and single mum of two, echoes Thomas' opinion and wants to relieve the pressure she puts on herself to do something different with her children every day. She says it's important to take time out, put work away, and spend one-on-one time with your children. This could be going to play in the park, or going swimming.Trips to local pools or lidos can cost around £6 for adults, and £3.50 for children.Abdur-Rashid says every night during the holidays she will play board games with her children, which blends quality time and fun. These can be picked up at local charity shops for very reasonable prices."You don't even have to leave the house for that," she says, "and they love it."3. Use what's available in your area Nilly Dahlia, a content creator and mum of three, says she prints out a six-week calendar with a range of activities for her kids during the holidays. As part of their "summer bucket list", they are planning to check out all the parks in the local area and she is prioritising low-cost activities throughout the summer. "I feel like there's this intense pressure to have Instagram-worthy holidays now," she says."What's wrong with just staying in the UK, staying out till sunset, riding your bike, just going to the river, like I did? I really want the kids to experience a nostalgic summer."Dahlia stresses there are many things on offer during the holidays that won't break the bank, such as free kids' meals in cafes and discounts on local travel. And there are often offers at bowling venues and cinemas, she says, while her family enjoys a movie night at home every Friday."They each have a bowl of popcorn and treats and we move the sofas into two rows so it's like a cinema."James Gray, communications and advocacy manager at Libraries Connected, says the summer holidays are also where libraries "come alive". He says libraries across the UK will hold the Summer Reading Challenge, encouraging kids to read more in a fun format, and many will be hosting events such as arts and crafts, performances and creative workshops, all for free. 4. Balance rest with some learningDahlia says she picks up books for her children to get them ready for the next school year. Her youngest will receive some chapter books to help them transition into Year 3, while her eldest is moving to secondary school, and Dahlia has prepped suitable books to bridge that gap from primary.She preps "summer baskets" which include puzzle books, reading books and snacks  to curb any boredom. "It's so important because by reading, they're still engaging their brain so they can go back to school in September, already having vocabulary in them."As a busy parent, Abdur-Rashid says she doesn't always have the time to do everything she'd like with her children, but structures their days to make sure they are always doing an activity. She allocates an hour a day for gaming which her boys enjoy, and then fills the rest of the time with playing, reading or writing. She also wants to foster a passion for reading in her kids, and allows them to not finish books they don't enjoy so reading doesn't become a "punishment".Image source, Tasneem Abdur-RashidImage caption, Author Tasneem Abdur-Rashid suggests parks and picnics for low-cost quality time with your childrenGavin Morgan, an education psychologist at University College London, says it's important to let children be "bored" during the holidays. "It's really important that they have opportunities to switch off from school and from that structure in order to experience and explore new things and get bored, because for some kids, that can really spark that creativity."For those entering exam years, Morgan says parents should have a conversation with their child about what they need to do and what suits them best. "The worst thing for parents to do is put their child under any kind of pressure, because they'll end up being switched off from learning," he says.He says parents should encourage their children to take a break from their education, so they return to school in September "feeling really confident and refreshed".5. Get ahead for the next holidays Thomas says she starts planning her summer budget well in advance. She does this by contributing a little bit of money every month into a "sinking fund" - a pot of money set aside for a specific purpose.This summer her budget is £500, and she sits down with her children to discuss how much they have budgeted and to brainstorm activities they can do together. "You've got that open dialogue, so they understand there's only a finite amount of money, and we've got a plan on how to do that best," she says.Thomas also uses cashback websites to get money back on things she has bought, which she says is "brilliant for hotels or travel". If you are planning a holiday, whether abroad or in the UK, Thomas stresses to plan and book in advance to get better deals. She also recommends looking at attractions within your local area before travelling further afield. Additional reporting by Hayley Clarke

schema.headline: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Summer of chaos' and 'water bosses' pay rises'
description: Pictures of tourists on a beach in France, with a huge cloud of black smoke from wildfires burning in the distance, are on several front pages. "Europ
body: Pictures of tourists on a beach in France, with a huge cloud of black smoke from wildfires burning in the distance, are on several front pages. "Europe ablaze" says the FT Weekend, external. "Summer of chaos" is the Daily Mirror's headline, external. It says thousands of British holidaymakers are facing huge queues to travel to mainland Europe, while fires rage.The Times says, external it's seen a report which says the UK is at a greater risk of blackouts because of the drive towards renewable energy. The paper says in the era of fossil fuel power plants, the national grid operator could easily monitor its output and balance demand and supply, minute by minute - but that's become much more difficult with the emergence of wind farms, solar panels and batteries. One whistleblower claims the grid operator is now "flying blind."On its front page the Daily Telegraph says, external Iran is sending its operatives to the UK in migrant boats. The paper says Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps controls some of the people smuggling routes across Europe. An unnamed Iranian official says the regime could easily make London unsafe if it wanted to. The Home Office has been approached for comment.According to FT Weekend, external, the new Chancellor, John Healey, is under mounting pressure to raise taxes or find savings, because the government's fiscal buffer has been eroded to a "razor thin level". The paper says renewed fighting in the Middle East has increased the cost of government borrowing, while Andy Burnham has made new spending commitments with measures to support households and small businesses.An investigation by the Daily Mail, external has found that some parents are being financially crippled, or driven to suicide, because of "massively inflated" child maintenance charges. The paper says "appalling blunders" by the Child Maintenance Service have led to people being overcharged several thousand pounds a month; some have lost their homes and at least two fathers have taken their own lives. The agency denies having significant issues with its IT system.And the Sun says, external Madonna is in talks to play a record three consecutive nights at BST Hyde Park in London next summer. If she does, the paper says, around 210,000 people are expected to attend, but sources close to her say nothing has been decided.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Summer of chaos' and 'water bosses' pay rises'

title: Tyson Fury vs Mariusz Wach: Briton wins low-key warm-up to keep Anthony Joshua fight on track
description: British heavyweight Tyson Fury stopped Mariusz Wach in a low-key bout in Thailand to keep a potential blockbuster fight with Anthony Joshua on track.
body: British heavyweight Tyson Fury stopped Mariusz Wach in a low-key bout in Thailand to keep a potential blockbuster fight with Anthony Joshua on track. The 37-year-old dominated for seven rounds at the Max Muay Thai Stadium in Pattaya - in front of no more than 1,500 fans - before the overmatched Wach, 46, retired on his stool at the start of the eighth. The 36th victory of his career moves Fury closer to a meeting with fellow Briton Joshua, who has his own comeback fight against Albanian Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia on Saturday."I went through my test tonight. Let's see if he can get through his," Fury said. Many expected 'the Gypsy King' to fly straight to Jeddah for Joshua's bout, with the pair potentially announcing their long-awaited showdown in the ring afterwards if Joshua wins.Instead, Fury said he was going home."I've got to face off with my wife. I've got to iron when I get home. I've been away for six out of the last seven months", he said. "I'm not going to Jeddah, I'm going home to my wife and kids. I'm going to regroup and hopefully we'll have a big fight signed next week."Questions still linger over where the all-British bout would take place, with Eddie Hearn saying Joshua's contract stipulates the UK, but industry whispers suggesting a venue in America."We'll head wherever we're going to head," Fury said."Who knows? It could be in Vegas, New York, Ireland, London. Who knows where the fight's going to be?"Fury's win over Wach was not broadcast live on any television or radio platform, and will instead form part of the third series of the Netflix reality show 'At Home With The Furys'.Fury has become a mainstream celebrity beyond boxing, with his outspoken personality, reality TV appearances and larger-than-life public image.But in Pattaya there was no pay-per-view build-up or millions watching from home.Earlier in the evening, the venue staged its regular programme of Muay Thai bouts before staff stripped away the canvas and transformed the ring for Fury's boxing card."We've all heard of the 'Thriller in Manila', you've heard of the 'Rumble in the Jungle' and you've heard of the punch-up in Pattaya," Fury said.There was something almost nostalgic about it all. A generation ago, boxing fans might have waited until the following morning to read the result in the newspapers.This time, reporters were refreshing social media, while the handful of journalists and YouTube channels inside the venue became the eyes and ears for everyone else.According to those updates, Fury controlled the opening rounds, although one clip posted on X showed Poland's Wach catching him with a right hand in the second.Another revealed pockets of empty seats - a striking contrast for a fighter who has packed Wembley Stadium with 96,000 fans and drawn 64,500 to Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.Another clip showed Fury, who said ticket profits would be donated to a local charity supporting disadvantaged children and students with disabilities, dictating the pace and repeatedly landing uppercuts at close range in the fifth.One reporter even claimed Fury paused to kiss Wach midway through the sixth round.It was not long before Wach and his corner had seen enough. Unable to withstand another three rounds of punishment, Wach was withdrawn to hand Fury his first stoppage victory since beating Derek Chisora in 2022.

schema.headline: Tyson Fury vs Mariusz Wach: Briton wins low-key warm-up to keep Anthony Joshua fight on track

title: Who could be the next Graham Norton, and does the BBC even need one?
description: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?Image caption, Winkleman steppd down from her chat show last w
body: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?Image caption, Winkleman steppd down from her chat show last week following its seven-episode runBySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporterWhen Lisa Kudrow appeared on The Claudia Winkleman Show earlier this year, she was visibly delighted to meet Linda from The Traitors. The Friends actress, probably the most famous guest the programme had during its seven-week run, said it was "thrilling" to meet one of the reality show's breakout stars, who she revealed had even inspired one of her own recent performances.As host of The Traitors, Winkleman was ideally placed to introduce the pair, resulting in the kind of wonderfully bizarre meeting of minds normally seen on The Graham Norton Show. But Winkleman's own chat show did not last long enough for any more unusual guest combinations on its teal sofa. The presenter quit last week after just one series, saying she was simply "too nervous to enjoy it". It had made sense for the BBC to commission The Claudia Winkleman Show, given the presenter's popularity on programmes such as Strictly.There's a different level of pressure, however, hosting a show with your own name above the door. Image caption, Lisa Kudrow (second left) said she was "thrilled" to meet Linda from the Traitors (far right) on the chat show"Everyone thought she could pull it off because she's smart and funny, but a chat show with multiple guests is very difficult to handle," the Telegraph's arts and entertainment editor, Anita Singh, tells BBC News."You have to marshall the conversation, give each guest equal time, help them to plug whatever they're plugging, then cue in whatever anecdote they've agreed beforehand with the researchers. Graham Norton makes that look deceptively easy."She adds: "I think if Claudia had done a couple more series she would have become better at it. But she's at her best when she's being spontaneous, and the format allows very little space for that."Winkleman's decision to quit surprised many. The viewing figures were lower than Norton's, but still respectable. The reviews from critics were mixed, rather than universally bad. The BBC confirmed it was Winkleman's decision to stop, and implied that they would've happily commissioned a second series - and possibly already had. "My understanding is they had made a deal beyond one season," says Deadline's Jake Kanter, who has reported on the talk show throughout. "How formal that was, I don't know. But there was an intention for it to continue."He adds: "I wholeheartedly believe her that this perhaps didn't work out because of her own concerns and anxiety around the hosting."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Winkleman's chat show was made by Graham Norton's production company So TelevisionFormer BBC One controller Peter Fincham, who hosts the TV podcast Insiders, likens it to the Davina McCall chat show he commissioned in 2006, which also ended after one series. "You have to remember, particularly chat shows where the presenter's name is in the title, it's very exposing for them," he tells BBC News. "Had Claudia Winkleman wanted to carry on with her chat show, it could have been a slow burn," he reflects. "But what she's done is rare, actually, for somebody to say, 'hmm, didn't really enjoy that, don't think I'll do it again'. "That says something very positive about her that you don't often see among presenters."Succession planningMany considered Winkleman, 54, to be chat show emperor Graham Norton's presumptive successor - not least because he seemed to be ushering her through himself.So Television, which Norton co-owns, also produced Winkleman's show, and it could have been a neat way for the company to retain work when Norton does eventually quit.Admittedly, Norton's show is not vanishing any time soon - he signed a new three-year deal with the BBC in 2025. He has also taken on several new projects, including a podcast, more novels, and a short-lived ITV game show, The Neighbourhood.But Norton, 63, has also spoken openly in recent years about working less. He reduced the number of chat show episodes he presents in 2022, and also stepped down from his Virgin Radio show two years later.Image source, BBC/So TelevisionImage caption, The BBC signed a new three-year deal with The Graham Norton Show in 2025The short life of The Claudia Winkleman Show could make the Norton succession plan a key issue for the BBC's incoming entertainment chief, Ed Havard. "This does leave the BBC with a problem if and when Graham decides to retire, because if Claudia can't do it, I don't know who can," says Singh."Graham doesn't want to do 52 weeks a year," Fincham notes, "so I'm sure the BBC would have been delighted to have another long-running chat show that you can balance with his, and they may have another try."Dozens of presenters would love the gig and many would be perfectly capable - Jack Whitehall did a solid job when he stood in for Norton previously, or Alan Carr could probably be tempted to return to his Chatty Man days. But the TV landscape is also littered with examples of cancelled chat shows. As well as Winkleman and McCall, Lily Allen and Charlotte Church also hosted series which didn't last long. Image caption, Winkleman will continue to host The Traitors and the forthcoming second series of its popular celebrity spin-offA cynic might say that the short life of Winkleman's series will have shown both her and the BBC that launching a new chat show is harder than it looks.But Kanter has a more nuanced interpretation, reflecting: "My instinct is that this was always a bit of an experiment. "Clearly it was something that Claudia wanted to do, and when you have a presenter at the peak of her powers, I think it's just good talent management to try and work together with that presenter on their dream project."He adds: "I'm sure all sides will walk away with their heads held high, and it was worth giving it a crack, I think."Do we still need chat shows?Personalities aside, there's the more existential question of whether the BBC even needs a new talk series, when there are now hundreds of other platforms where celebrities can go to promote their product. Stars can just as easily appear on YouTube strands such as Snack Wars or Hot Ones as a TV chat show, or spend as much time at press junkets being interviewed by TikTokers as legacy media outlets. Talent agents know that seeing Hollywood stars talking to a lovable and sweary East London pensioner, external known as Grime Gran, or playing a game of Would You Rather, external with LadBible, is just as likely to generate publicity as traditional interviews.Singh highlights that clips from programmes such as Norton's often go viral too, but adds: "I don't think the public is craving another TV chat show."Think back to the most memorable encounters from the heyday of chat shows," she says. "They were one-on-one: Parkinson with Muhammad Ali; Wogan with George Best or David Icke. "Those long-form interviews have moved to podcasts now, where celebrities find it easy to be open and essentially treat them as an extended therapy session. "And the most entertaining celebrity interviews around are on Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date. Compared to content like that, a chat show in a TV studio seems quite old-fashioned."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dimoldenberg interviews stars on Chicken Shop Date and now serves as the Oscars' red carpet reporterNorton's show clearly still delivers huge value for the BBC, and Kanter says the the "chat show format remains strong" and is a "really important part of the BBC One schedule"."It sprinkles a bit of stardust, it's appointment to view, I think people enjoy that it's a Friday night and they can tune in for some entertainment, it performs well online, it's an engine for clips and viral moments, and that's something that's to be valued in this attention economy," he notes.And, speaking from experience, Fincham concludes he is "not a big fan of succession plans" anyway."I ran BBC One between 2005 and 2007," he recalls, "and at that time, a regular conversation was 'What's the succession plan for David Attenborough?' "That was 20 years ago, and I can't help noticing he's still presenting programmes today. So beware of the assumption that a succession plan is needed. "And Graham Norton, if he chooses to continue, has got plenty more in the tank."

schema.headline: Who could be the next Graham Norton, and does the BBC even need one?

title: BuzzBallz are 'greenwashing' say recycling experts
description: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statem
body: BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.BuzzBallz's UK's mission statement, which was deleted after the BBC contacted the company about this story, said it "loves our planet as much as we love a good cocktail" and partnered with TerraCycle to ensure its packaging gets recycled. However, TerraCycle, which involves consumers collecting packaging and sending it to be recycled, only runs the BuzzBallz scheme in the United States. BuzzBallz's UK FAQs, now also deleted, stated: "Yes, our packaging is recyclable. Please recycle your empties where local facilities allow."But no local facilities anywhere in the UK allow BuzzBallz to be recycled, said Adam Herriott, the head of packaging at WRAP."They're a mix of two very recyclable materials that put together makes an unrecyclable format."No local authorities will accept these at the kerbside."If they end up at a sorting facility, they could end up contaminating the plastic stream because of the metals in there and that could be very problematic for plastics recyclers that get into the machinery."But why should people care if their drink packaging is not recyclable?Even the shape of the BuzzBallz make it harder to be recycled because they can roll on the conveyor belts at the sorting facilities, said Herriott.  Among the machinery used, scanners can identify it in one position, but by the time air jets are used to separate it into the right recycling stream, it could have moved, meaning it could contaminate other streams. "It's definitely one of the villains of recycling," said Ambarish Mitra, co-founder of Greyparrot, a waste analytics company which helps recovery facilities. He said BuzzBallz have "have no recovery route in the current system" and "is a huge pet peeve for our customers and us".After analysing a plastic recover facility in Manchester with a processing capacity of 35,000 tonnes of plastic a year, for six months, the company found that BuzzBallz contaminated recycled plastic 66% of the time. "Once in the plastic stream, the aluminium reduces the quality of the recycled plastic, while the colour pigments can lower the recycled plastic bale's value."This isn't a recycling problem. It's a packaging problem."BuzzBallz refused to comment.James Piper, co-host of the Talking Rubbish podcast, co-owner of Ecosurety, said he dislikes BuzzBallz because of how difficult they are to recycle. "Every stage of the recycling journey has been designed around predictable packaging," Piper said. "When people come along and say, 'I'm going to make something different for marketing reasons', they are automatically making it more difficult for the recycler.""There's nothing environmentally positive about mixing packaging types."He said the BuzzBallz 'biggies' which have a plastic screw top lid is completely recyclable."Anyone can say on their website 'this is recyclable where your council allows'. But if no council allows it, then it doesn't mean anything," he said. BuzzBallz said: "We very recently went through a global website update and the information pertaining to TerraCycle recycling for BuzzBallz was incorrectly copied and does not apply to the UK market as of today. "We apologise for the oversight and have since updated our website to reflect the correct position for UK consumers."The company refused to comment on the now-deleted UK FAQs stating its packaging was recyclable.

title: Police declare 'major incident' as wind change increases Cairngorms wildfire risk
description: Police Scotland has declared a major incident as emergency services continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Pa
body: Police Scotland has declared a major incident as emergency services continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.The force said it followed "a significant change in weather conditions" which has increased the risk of fire spreading towards the village of Nethy Bridge.All Nethy Bridge residents have been evacuated as a precaution to allow emergency services to continue their response.But a local resident told the BBC the wildfire should have been declared a major incident sooner and the lack of communication from authorities had been "pretty poor".The BBC has contacted the Scottish government and Police Scotland for comment.First Minister John Swinney, who held a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience room early on Saturday, said additional police resources were being deployed to assist with the Nethy Bridge evacuation. Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.Supt Judy Hill said weather conditions "experienced within the Cairngorms over the last 24 hours have added further complexities to this situation"."With evidence suggesting the fire is spreading towards Nethy Bridge, the decision has been taken to declare a major incident and evacuate residents as a precaution."She said additional police resources were being deployed to help contact those who need to leave their properties.

schema.headline: Police declare 'major incident' as wind change increases Cairngorms wildfire risk

title: 'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's concert for rescue dogs didn't go according to planByMusic correspondentEvery band has to earn its str
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's concert for rescue dogs didn't go according to planByMusic correspondentEvery band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single."We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin."It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech."The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time."We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."Image source, Dean BradshawImage caption, Muna in 2026 (L-R): Naomi McPherson, Katie Gavin and Josette MaskinNowadays, that canine catastrophe is a dot in Muna's rear-view mirror. Over the past decade, they've become one of the most compelling live bands around – a little bit punk, a little bit electronic, a little bit 80s, eminently watchable and endlessly impressive.Fans include Harry Styles and Taylor Swift, who handpicked the trio (completed by guitarist/producer Naomi McPherson) to support them on tour.They were won over by sing-along anthems like I Know A Place, a great big exuberant hug for the LGBTQ community; and the more introspective Stayaway, where Gavin locks herself in her bedroom to avoid anything - friends, music, drink - that could tempt her back into the arms of an ex.In 2020, all their momentum nearly came to a crashing halt when RCA Records dropped the band, citing pandemic-era cost-cutting."That's obviously one where we had to put our heads together and be like, 'OK, we want to continue doing this. Let's just make an album and we'll figure it out'," says McPherson.'We need movement'That album, simply titled Muna, was eventually released by indie star Phoebe Bridgers, who swooped in to sign the band to her Saddest Factory label in 2021."Phoebe's manager had made it very clear that if we were ever single, she'd be interested in working with us," Gavin told the BBC at the time.Bridgers also provided guest vocals on Silk Chiffon, a freewheeling sapphic love song that became Muna's breakthrough single.It pegged the band, in its members' own words, as "the queer joy mini-skirt rollerblade, external" crew - but their music has always dug deeper than that.I Know A Place, for example, was written as a response to the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting, acknowledging the fragility of the communal LGBTQ spaces it celebrated.Their fourth album, Dancing On The Wall, is their most powerful yet.The music is darker. The lyrics hit harder. Ostensibly anchored to the dancefloor, it's a record that uses dance music to shake the listener out of complacency."I think it was a response to a feeling of helplessness in this moment in time that can lead to paralysis," says Gavin."Movement is what we need right now, and we also need to feel powerful and to connect to our sources of energy. The tempo of this album helps with that."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The band are best seen live: "We were super lucky to hit at the right time to be able to play tiny venues and work our way up to where we are now," says McPhersonThe standout, lyrically speaking, is Big Stick. A critique of American imperialism, it's written from the perspective of Big Brother, who "can make you want anything that I want you to" – from war in Gaza to the militarisation of US police forces."And If you've got a problem with it, you could end up in jail," Gavin seethes as militaristic synths patrol the beat."I think sometimes people want to go to concerts to feel a brief reprieve from the horrors of the world around them, but right now the horrors are so pervasive that what I found myself wanting was a container to express my anger together with other people," says the singer."It's an emotional release that I think we are often denied because we have to read tragedies in the news every day and then keep our heads down and work."Given the polarised state of political discourse in the US, did they have any misgivings about releasing the song?"Maybe this is actually stupid, but I don't think it was a big decision for us," says Maskin."We have always been a political band, and we've always been super open with what we believe in, so it really wasn't a question."Elsewhere, the album transports the listener to sweaty, laser-lit nightclubs, where unyielding rhythms fuel feelings of "horniness and heartache".The title track is full of thwarted desire, as Gavin tries and fails to get the attention of a girl who constantly leaves her dangling. Wannabeher, meanwhile, is a sticky, sleazy track about being so completely besotted with someone that you start to blur the boundaries between where your personality ends and theirs begins."I think that's a canon gay experience, where you don't know whether you want to be with someone or you actually want to be them," laughs Maskin.Image caption, The band formed at university in 2013, with McPherson producing all of their musicEastside Girls, meanwhile, is a tender depiction of Muna's neighbourhood, lovingly lampooning the staples of LA hipster culture – astrology, polyamory, roommate dramas and "negronis with the nice gin"."It's a city that's run by sunshine," says McPherson, who moved to LA from her native San Diego."It's bohemian but it's also populated by some of the richest people in the world. It's a strange dichotomy."The song's chorus is a masterclass in melody and, in Maskin's words, "smacks you in the face". It takes its place among Muna's most irresistible hooks (see also, Number One Fan, Stayaway, What I Want) – which all stem from Gavin's love of classic pop."She's been writing songs since she was eight years old, so it's a well-honed skill," says McPherson."I think it's a benefit of my obsessive personality, honestly," says Gavin."I am constantly searching for the next big chorus, and will probably always be. Also, once I have a seed in my head for a song that feels promising, it really has a hold on me and won't let me go until I feel I've done it justice." (Wannabeher, McPherson reveals, is the final version of a song that began 11 years ago.)"I will say," Gavin adds, "one random tip is writing in motion - walking, driving, rollerblading, anything like that."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Muna's tour hits the UK this November, in their biggest venues to dateThat explains why Muna's music always feels propulsive. "If you're not sweating after the first song, come on," laughs McPherson.With an ever-growing fanbase, they'll play their biggest ever tour this autumn, titled the Gets So Hot Tour after the album's opening track – although the band previously joked it would be called "The Midwest Princess, Midnight Sun and the Eras Tour as Well", before abandoning the idea for copyright reasons.A decade into their career, they're playing to "crowds we could never have imagined", while witnessing the genre labelled as "queer pop" expand into the mainstream, with artists like Chappell Roan, Renée Rapp, Lil Nas X and Troye Sivan all achieving crossover success."I do feel we were at the cusp of the reclamation of the word 'queer'," says Maskin."To us, it's actually a celebratory term, because it's inclusive, it includes everybody in the LGBTQI+ community."It came from academia first, the idea of queer theory," says McPherson, who admits the band were initially divided on whether to be open about their sexuality."We were reticent to come out of the closet in the hipster Pitchfork era of 2010 and 2011. We wanted to be mysterious and be closeted, and Katie was the one who encouraged us not to, and to just be ourselves. And we've only become more ourselves."Even so, the label can be restrictive. Muna want their music to be universal."The subject matter we write about is queer in its essence, and so are our life experiences," says McPherson."The issue that we struggle with is wanting that to also be accepted as just a human experience, as well – especially in these times of great repression."If anyone can do it, Muna can. Just don't let them play for your pets.

schema.headline: 'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig

title: The human cost of South Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveries
description: 'It eats away at my body': The human cost of S Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveriesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, South Korea's hug
body: 'It eats away at my body': The human cost of S Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveriesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, South Korea's huge delivery industry, powered by thousands of warehouse workers and riders, is under scrutinyByJake Kwon, Leehyun Choi and Hosu LeeReporting fromSeoulA week before her son died Park Mi-suk asked him to quit his job.For more than a year, the 27-year-old had been working overnight shifts at a warehouse for the country's largest online retailer, Coupang. He steered pallet movers with stacks of plastic bins and cardboard boxes across the sprawling space.In that time, Park says, her son lost 15kg and often complained of how tired he was.But Jang Deok-jun refused to quit. He compared his job to being on a seesaw: if he stepped down, his co-workers would struggle to keep going.The following week, Park found him unconscious and hunched over in the bath. "We pulled him out and performed first aid. We rushed him to hospital, where they declared him dead."Jang died of a heart attack. The state-run insurer that covers healthcare for workers, Comwel, blamed his death on overwork following an investigation.Park wishes she had noticed Jang's exhaustion sooner. "I didn't pay attention to my son's words, so I lost my son. But I hope others won't repeat the same mistake."Jang died in 2020 but six years on, Park is still fighting to end what she believes is the reason for his death: night-time deliveries.Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Jang Deok-jun was 27 years old when he died of a heart attackJang died as deliveries surged during the pandemic, which was often cited to explain his workload. But the working conditions for warehouse and delivery workers have been the subject of a growing national debate, with their union claiming that suspected deaths from overwork have continued.Night-time deliveries have become ubiquitous in hyper-connected South Korea, where shoppers are guaranteed delivery by 07:00 for orders placed before midnight. This convenience is thanks to a huge overnight workforce, from warehouse workers like Jang to delivery drivers.Several companies compete to offer speedy, cheap deliveries but the biggest is Coupang. Founded by a Korean-American, it became synonymous with online shopping in South Korea after 2015, when it started offering fresh produce overnight. It has grown to have an unrivalled network of warehouses and delivery trucks, with nearly 100,000 employees across the business.But increasingly, this industry is under scrutiny.Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Jang's mother Park Mi-suk says workers like her son are becoming invisibleBetween 2020 and May 2026, Comwel ruled that 46 warehouse and delivery workers, including Jang, died of a stroke or heart disease that count as work-related deaths. Jang aside, it's unclear how many of them worked overnight shifts.Comwel did not say how many of these cases were also investigated for the role of overwork, which only happens if the family asks for it in their claim. And not every case is referred to Comwel in the first place, so the data can be patchy.Previously Comwel data suggested that day-time delivery workers died of overwork and accidents at a higher rate than those who work overnight. But that is now questioned by those who say night-time deliveries are expanding fast, and there is not enough data to fully document their impact yet. The workers' union also argues that the latter is more harmful to health in the long-term.Night-time work is a probable cause of cancer globally, according to the UN's cancer research body, external. "Not only that, evidence has been accumulating that it also raises the risk of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and mental illness," says Kang Mo-yeol, professor of occupational medicine at the Catholic University of Korea.South Korea doesn't limit overnight working hours, unlike in the UK, where night-time delivery drivers cannot work more than 10 out of 24 hours. The Korean delivery workers' union called for a ban on overnight deliveries in 2025, but the union for Coupang's drivers says nearly all of their members prefer working at night. Some have children, elderly or ill family members to care for during the day and, more importantly, it pays better.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Coupang is the biggest of South Korea's online retailers "I can't do this for life because it eats away at my body," says Kim, a Coupang driver on a sub-contract, who did not want to share his real name. But he adds that his monthly salary of around 7m won ($4,600; £3,430) - nearly double the national average - makes it worth it.When the BBC met him at 22:00, he had already loaded his truck for the first round of deliveries.Driving through the narrow streets of Incheon city, west of the capital Seoul, he explains that he works from 21:00 to 07:00, five to six days a week.His schedule does not allow for a break. Every time the truck stops, he runs, package in hand. Nearly all drivers are paid by the number of packages they deliver and if they fail to make all deliveries by 07:00, they risk losing their "territory" to a competitor, he says.At first, his pregnant wife was scared he might fall asleep at the wheel. But he is used to it now, he insists, and he finds it easier to navigate the night's empty streets."We choose to deliver overnight for the money," Kim says. The way he sees it, those who are saying overnight deliveries should stop because they affect his health are ignoring the choice he has made. Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Kim said he is making good money as an overnight delivery driver, but his wife is worried he will fall asleep at the wheelBut men like Kim are becoming invisible, Jang's mother Park says, as the demand for fast deliveries grows, normalising the industry.Park spoke to the BBC outside Coupang's headquarters in Seoul's office district of Songpa. Standing alone in front of the gate, she told staff streaming out for lunch to remember her son and others like him. Few paid attention.Park says one of the challenges is how hard it is to hold employers accountable in cases like Jang's. She says it was on her to prove that her son had died from overwork, and Coupang was obligated to provide records, including security camera footage, to Comwel, but not her. After months of leaning on lawmakers and government agencies, she received Jang's work log and relevant CCTV footage.In the months before his death, Jang's working hours met the bar for how South Korean law defines deaths related to overwork: heart attacks or brain strokes after an average 60-hour-week over 12 weeks, or 64 hours a week in the four weeks leading up to death. Jang's overnight hours counted 30% more towards the calculation, according to Comwel's rules.Image source, BBC/Hosu LeeImage caption, Park outside Coupang's headquarters in Seoul, where she has been trying to draw attention to Jang's case As Park continued her fight, local media published what Coupang's former chief privacy officer claimed was a conversation with Chairman Bom Kim. In the leaked chat, Kim orders the executive to remove mentions of Jang "working hard" from internal reports: a phrase several employees used to describe Jang's final shift. Coupang called it a "groundless" claim by a disgruntled former executive.But the union accused the firm of covering up evidence and filed a criminal complaint. The police launched an investigation into Coupang in December 2025. Coupang denies the accusation, saying it had submitted everything that was requested and had fully cooperated with Comwel's investigation.By then, another high-profile case was in the headlines. Oh Seung-yong, 34, died after crashing his truck into a pole during a delivery run. It was an "occupational death", or work played a role, Comwel ruled.Oh's sister told parliament his work log showed that he had been working six days a week, more than 11 hours a day, and mostly at night. According to her, when their father had died days earlier, Oh delivered orders for another four hours before coming to hospital. He worked for a logistics company contracted by Coupang.Coupang says it restricts its employees to working for under 52 hours and gives sub-contracted drivers the full weekend off every two weeks. But the union alleges that this was not enforced by Oh's employer.The firm added that it fully pays for health check-ups for direct employees and sub-contracted drivers, and "has never had a single industrial accident death, which is the best safety record in the entire global logistics industry".Image source, SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Coupang boss Harold Rogers at South Korea's parliament Coupang CEO Harold Rogers was summoned to parliament in December 2025 over the deaths of Jang and Oh, as well as to answer for a recent data breach at his firm, involving 37.5 million users. The country's largest ever breach, it earned them a record $410m fine.During the televised hearing, Park demanded that Coupang's Chairman Kim be held accountable for her son's death, while Oh's sister asked for an apology from Rogers. He said he was "sorry" and offered his "deepest condolences". When Oh's sister pressed further, he was silent.The investigation into Coupang has also raised key questions for President Lee Jae Myung, who has a disability in his left arm from an old injury at a factory. He made it one of his priorities to reduce workplace injuries and deaths.Stories like Jang's and Oh's resonate deeply in South Korea, where gruelling work hours are no anomaly. It has one of the highest rates of workplace deaths among developed countries, a grim statistic it has been trying to improve for decades.The government has capped weekly work hours at 52 and passed a law to jail executives for negligence leading to workplace deaths. To break Coupang's stranglehold, the governing party even proposed relaxing existing restrictions so more retailers can deliver overnight. But the bill angered unions, activists and Park, who say the challenge goes beyond Coupang.Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Six years on from 27-year-old Jang's death, his mother still has his belongings"I've been haunting the streets since my son died," Park says.Because of all the time spent fighting for compensation and answers, she was forced to close her furniture-making business. She could no longer afford to live in her old home and moved to a rental apartment in Daegu city.She has kept all of Jang's belongings, including his collection of action figures. They sit in a box in her new apartment. She isn't ready to say goodbye yet, or to give up her fight.Recalling how Jang compared his work to riding a seesaw, where he held down one end, she says she sees it differently now. Jang and tens of thousands of workers like him are on one side for the convenience of the consumers on the other end, she says. "I hope we don't become a society where we close our eyes to others' sacrifice for a little convenience."

schema.headline: The human cost of South Korea's ultra-convenient overnight deliveries

title: More than 220,000 evacuated in France and Spain due to wildfires
description: French authorities have ordered the evacuation of almost 60,000 people near Bordeaux, taking the total number of people told to flee wildfires in Fran
body: French authorities have ordered the evacuation of almost 60,000 people near Bordeaux, taking the total number of people told to flee wildfires in France and Spain to more than 220,000. Around 200,000 people have been evacuated in south-west France in the Gironde and Landes regions. French President Emmanuel Macron has mobilised the military to assist the response.Meanwhile, a fire near Madrid is "beyond the capacity" of firefighters to contain, Spanish officials have warned, after three fires west of the capital merged into a single blaze.Spain's government has declared a national emergency, with 25,000 people told to evacuate and almost 40,000 told to stay indoors.Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described it as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts. In Spain, local emergency services said wildfires were moving towards the municipalities of Robledo de Chavela and Fresnedillas de la Olivia, around 50km (31 miles) from the capital."The wildfire is at its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain," Carlos Novillo, the Madrid regional government's emergency management chief, told reporters."It's not possible to attack the fire in that area, so defensive measures are being taken," he added.The mayor of El Tiemblo, one of the affected areas in Ávila, said flames spread from Navaluenga to the Iruelas Valley - a distance of about 20km (12 miles) - in less than half an hour. "It was horrific," Arturo Varas González told laSexta.At least 6,000 hectares of land have burned in the Madrid region, while the Ávila blaze has consumed almost 9,000 hectares, according to officials.Eight municipalities have been evacuated, including Chapinería, Navas del Rey, Colmenar del Arroyo, Fresnedillas de la Oliva, Robledo de Chavela, Aldea del Fresno, Navalagamella and Zarzalejo.Several other towns, including San Martín de Valdeiglesias, Pelayos de la Presa and Villa del Prado, remain under lockdown.Ecologio Cabrera, 86, was forced to flee his village west of Madrid. "If you don't run from it and you try to face it, it devours you," he told AFP news agency from a sports hall in the village of Vilamanta where hundreds of evacuees have sought refuge.His family tried to save their home by spraying it with garden hoses until firefighters arrived. "They arrived and told everybody to get out... I have never experienced anything like this."Madrid's regional president Ayuso said the situation was "completely unusual and catastrophic," with the priority being saving lives.Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will visit the zone's emergency coordination centre early on Saturday, his administration said.Earlier on Friday, Sánchez said people were "living through a dramatic situation" and urged citizens to take great care.The Civil Guard has arrested one person and is investigating another over the Burgohondo fire, which officials said could have been caused by negligence involving heavy machinery used when a period of restrictions were in place, local media reported.In south-west France, authorities have evacuated around 200,000 people after wildfires ripped through the Gironde and Landes regions.In the early hours of Saturday, four towns near Bordeaux were evacuated "as a precaution". The towns were Saint-Médard-en-Jalles, Saint-Jean d'Illac, Martignas-sur-Jalles, and Saint-Aubin de Médoc, which together have a population of 58,400 residents. The Gironde blaze, described by local prefect Sophie Brocas as an "XXL fire", has burned through more than 19,000 hectares (46,000 acres) of forest and destroyed about 80 homes.Officials evacuated the entire Cap Ferret peninsula on the south-west coast, with hundreds escaping by boat after flames swept through the popular tourist destination. The area has a year-round population of just under 8,000 people, but numbers can increase 10 fold during the summer holiday season. Fire and rescue chief Marc Vermeulen said conditions were more severe than during the devastating fires that hit the region in 2022, with drought enabling the blaze to continue spreading through the night."We have never seen a convective fire of this magnitude," France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told French broadcaster TF1, adding that around 50 firefighters had been injured.He said the blaze was "self-sustaining" and changing direction, with the fire moving east towards Bordeaux on Friday evening."We are going to reorganise our response so we can fight it from the ground and prevent it from advancing toward Bordeaux," he said.Further south, another wildfire near Biscarrosse in the Landes region forced more than 23,000 people to evacuate homes, campsites, a nursing home and a summer camp.Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul said the fire would not be extinguished by the end of Friday, with winds reaching 50km/h (31mph) and temperatures of 36-37C.Philippe de Gonneville, the mayor of one of the worst-affected areas, Lège-Cap Ferret, said the region had "faced extreme weather conditions for the last month and a half" with no rain and above-average temperatures."It's unheard of," he said. "Neither we nor the firefighters have seen anything like it."President Macron described the wildfire situation in the country as "very tense", particularly in Gironde.He said France had activated the European Union's civil protection mechanism and will receive reinforcements, including two Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia.The European Union has deployed aircraft and helicopters to support firefighting efforts in Spain and France, as much of southern Europe grapples with repeated heatwaves and prolonged drought.Europe is the fastest-warming continent, heating at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service.Hotter, drier conditions are leaving vegetation with less moisture, creating fuel that enables wildfires to ignite and spread more quickly.A spark is still needed - most often from human activity, whether accidental or deliberate, or from lightning - but extreme heat, dry vegetation and strong winds can make fires burn faster and become much harder to contain.Wildfires have burned more land in Europe already this year than the annual average for the past two decades, according to the European Forest Fire Information System.The European Environment Agency has said "climate change has increased forest fire risk across Europe", with the greatest danger expected in southern Europe.

schema.headline: More than 220,000 evacuated in France and Spain due to wildfires

title: How do Man City deal with the Rodri dilemma?
description: How do Manchester City manage the Rodri dilemma?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Rodri captained Spain to their World Cup final victory over A
body: How do Manchester City manage the Rodri dilemma?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Rodri captained Spain to their World Cup final victory over ArgentinaByFootball tactics correspondentManchester City are in flux.Replacing a manager after 10 years is no easy feat, let alone when there appears to be a squad overhaul too.Four of the starters in City's Treble-winning side of 2022-23 - Manuel Akanji, Nathan Ake, Bernardo Silva and John Stones - have left this summer, with the Blues signing £116m Elliot Anderson and promising 17-year-old Jeremy Monga.And the changes might not end there.Fresh from captaining Spain to World Cup victory, Rodri will head for back surgery on Monday with just a year left on his contract, amid increasing speculation about his future.It is not clear how long the 30-year-old will spend on the sidelines, but one thing new boss Enzo Maresca was clear on in his first news conference was that he wants to keep him.But with reports that Real Madrid are "operating on the basis" of Rodri joining them,, external what do City do?Will they look to cash in when Rodri returns to fitness, or keep to Maresca's stance?And how might Maresca's midfield operate - with or without Rodri?What's the background?When Rodri returned from an anterior cruciate ligament injury last year, there will have been plenty who wondered whether he would return to the Ballon d'Or-winning levels he had reached at his peak.Pep Guardiola - the man Maresca has replaced - said last October: "In the World Cup, he will be the best Rodri, and next season he will be the best Rodri."Guardiola was proved right on the first count. Not only did Rodri captain Spain to World Cup success but he was also awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.Maresca was unequivocal when asked for his view on Friday."I think every manager wants to have Rodri because he is a top player," he said."But now, surgery on Monday... he needs a holiday... he needs to rest and recover and then he will be back with us."The plan seems clear, therefore - look to retain one of the best players in world football rather than sell him.But there will have to be contingencies in place.One of these will be the presence of Anderson, while City are monitoring 18-year-old Lille midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi, who impressed for Morocco in the World Cup.What does a Maresca midfield look like?To understand how Rodri, Anderson and someone like Bouaddi might come together, it is key to understand Maresca's game model.As a disciple of positional play, he draws comparisons between his football and chess."There are a lot of similarities," Maresca said. "The most important is positional play and strategy."For a coach, it's important to have the mentality of a chess player: develop a plan, study counter-moves, choose the arrangement of the pieces."Maresca's strategy has largely been rooted in an on-the-ball shape that looks like a 3-2-2-3.One of Rodri's most useful qualities in a Maresca side would be his ability to move between these predefined positions on the pitch.Throughout the World Cup, for example, we saw him drop into the backline when former City team-mate Aymeric Laporte pushed up with the ball.Naturally, Rodri spent most of the game in a holding midfield position, but when space opened up he was more than capable of pushing forward too.Image gallerySkip image galleryImage caption, In the World Cup final against Argentina, we saw the many positional rotations Rodri enabled. Here he is playing as a third centre-back as Spain build out from the back. Slide 1 of 3, A screen grab from Spain against Argentina in the World Cup final showing Rodri in a centre-back position., In the World Cup final against Argentina, we saw the many positional rotations Rodri enabled. Here he is playing as a third centre-back as Spain build out from the back.At their best, Maresca's sides use rotations of players within the 3-2-2-3. His innovation often comes in the form of creating this shape in new ways.Defending as a 4-4-2 before attacking in the 3-2-2-3, it was Stones who stepped up from centre-back into a midfield pair with Rodri during City's Treble-winning season, when Maresca was assistant manager.At Chelsea, one of Maresca's more unique tweaks involved playing Moises Caicedo at right-back. Defending with a back four before again attacking in a 3-2-2-3 shape, Caicedo would move from right-back into one of the holding midfield positions.Image caption, In the build-up to Chelsea's opening goal against Liverpool in 2025, Caicedo (highlighted) has inverted from a right-back position when defending to a central midfield position when attacking. Maresca's 3-box-3 shape - also known as 3-2-2-3 - is clearly seen hereWhere does Anderson fit in?Here is where the signing of Anderson makes such sense.Throughout his career, the 23-year-old has played in every midfield and attacking position at one point. For England, he has frequently dropped into defence to form a back five out of possession.Alongside Rodri, Anderson would be able to sit deep, allowing the Spaniard to showcase his attacking quality - and vice versa.Both players would be capable of taking turns in dropping deeper to maintain the balance of the team if strong carriers of the ball like Marc Guehi or Josko Gvardiol were to push forward.Piggy-backing on the success of Rodri's work with Bernardo Silva, City would hope their new versatile and combative winger-turned-holding-midfielder will bring about similar success.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, According to Transfermarkt, Anderson has played 44% of his career games in central midfield, 22% in attacking midfield, 19% in defensive midfield and 16% in wide positions, with even one appearance as a centre-forwardBouaddi - like Anderson - has played in a number of roles, more specifically holding midfield, right-back and centre-back.His ability to occupy those positions - with strong defending and elegance on the ball - replicates some of the work Stones did for City.The club are looking at young and intelligent footballers capable of playing for possession-heavy sides. More important, however, is their ability to be positionally versatile across the roles Maresca's system demands.When numerous players can move into any of the positions that open up, it can result in a structured yet fluid team that become harder for the opposition to defend against – think Luis Enrique's Paris St-Germain.But this takes both time and tutelage.What if Rodri goes?City will look better with Rodri, who possesses an understanding of positioning, speed and risk that Anderson and future signings may take time to grasp.After all, it took Rodri a few seasons to navigate the change in environment under Fernandinho's wing.But should he go, Maresca has previously shown an impressive ability to recognise positions players could move into but haven't yet done: Stones into holding midfield, Caicedo into full-back, Marc Cucurella into attacking midfield... the list goes on.Whether or not City further bolster their squad, Maresca will hope to have a greater number of pieces to place on his board - a departure from Guardiola's approach of maintaining a smaller squad.That factor - and this holds true whether or not Rodri stays - should give City's new boss a greater chance of landing on a working formula next season.

schema.headline: How do Man City deal with the Rodri dilemma?
